title: A presentation plan that leaves room for your voice
excerpt: Prepare your message, agree on support, and handle questions without making fluency the goal.

sections.heading: Build a message you can return to
sections.body:
Begin with the idea you want your audience to remember. Write three supporting points and one example for each. A small cue card can hold these headings, so you can return to your message after a pause without restarting the whole presentation.

Rehearse for familiarity with your material. You do not need to memorise every syllable or repeat a sentence until it comes out smoothly. Try explaining the same point to one trusted person, then decide whether a larger practice audience would be useful.

sections.heading: Agree on the room before the day
sections.body:
Ask the teacher or organiser about timing, questions, and the assessment criteria. If useful, request extra speaking time or questions after each section. These are requests to discuss with your institution; availability depends on its arrangements.

  • Check the microphone and where your notes will sit.
  • Decide whether you want to mention stuttering at the start.
  • Ask a friend to help collect audience questions if that suits you.

sections.heading: Keep ownership of the presentation
sections.body:
You can pause, look at your notes, and continue. You may say, “I need a moment; I will finish this point.” If someone interrupts, try, “I will come to that after this example.” These are optional scripts, not a requirement to explain yourself.

Afterward, record whether you communicated your main idea and what support helped. Stuttering during the talk does not erase the preparation or the knowledge you shared. Choose one useful change for next time, rather than grading every word.

title: Preparing for a viva or oral exam
excerpt: A practical checklist for discussing assessment needs and organising your answers.

sections.heading: Ask about the format early
sections.body:
Find out how long answers should be, whether you can use rough paper, and what the examiner is assessing. Contact your teacher or student support office before the exam if you need an arrangement. Explain the effect of time pressure in concrete terms, rather than assuming everyone understands stuttering.

A possible email is: “I stutter and may need additional time to complete spoken answers. Could we discuss how my subject knowledge will be assessed and what arrangements are available?” Ask for the agreed plan in writing and check whether documentation is needed.

sections.heading: Use an answer structure
sections.body:
For a technical question, practise a simple sequence: definition, explanation, example. For a calculation, name the rule, show the steps, and interpret the result. You can practise selecting the next idea without practising a particular speaking pattern.

  • Ask the examiner to repeat an unclear question.
  • Take the thinking time the format allows.
  • Use permitted diagrams to support your explanation.
  • Tell the examiner when you have more to add.

sections.heading: Keep the review about learning
sections.body:
After a mock viva, ask a friend to comment on the correctness and organisation of your answer. Ask them to let you finish before offering feedback. Avoid treating the number of repetitions as your mark.

If an agreed arrangement is missed, make a factual note and contact the relevant university office. The examples here are planning suggestions, not a statement of legal entitlements in Bangladesh; confirm your own institution’s procedures.

title: Making phone calls with less guesswork
excerpt: Prepare a short call outline and a backup route while keeping the choice to speak yours.

sections.heading: Write the job of the call
sections.body:
Before dialling, write the reason for calling, any reference number, and the question you need answered. Keep your name and contact information nearby. A short outline is often easier to use than a full script that feels difficult to change.

Decide whether you want to say, “I stutter, so please give me a moment to finish.” You can also ask the person not to disconnect during a silence. Disclosure is your choice; you do not owe a stranger your history.

sections.heading: Plan for the practical interruptions
sections.body:
If a receptionist transfers you, ask for the department’s name and a direct contact in case the line drops. If you are asked to repeat something, you can repeat only the needed information. You do not have to restart the whole conversation.

  • Choose a place where you can hear clearly.
  • Write down the answer while it is fresh.
  • Ask for a booking or reference number.
  • Confirm any next step before ending the call.

sections.heading: Use the communication route that works today
sections.body:
Email, web forms, and asking someone to support a call can be useful options. Using them is not a failure. If making a call matters to you, choose a manageable one and arrange a supportive listener for practice.

A successful call is one that moves your task forward. Note what you found out and whether the other person gave you time. If calls remain distressing, bring one specific example to a qualified therapist and discuss the kind of support you want.

title: Job and internship interviews when you stutter
excerpt: Show your skills, prepare useful examples, and discuss the interview format in advance.

sections.heading: Prepare evidence of what you can do
sections.body:
Choose three examples from a project, course, or team activity. For each, write the situation, your action, the result, and one thing you learned. Technical applicants can prepare a diagram or a short explanation of a design choice where the format permits it.

Practise answering variations of a question so that you can stay with the idea rather than a memorised sentence. A supportive mock interviewer should wait until you finish, then comment on the substance of your answer.

sections.heading: Discuss the format if you want support
sections.body:
You may contact the recruiter to explain that you stutter and ask for time to complete spoken answers. For an online interview, clarify whether you can use the chat for technical terms or reference numbers. Ask what arrangements are possible instead of assuming the organisation has a particular policy.

An optional opening is: “I stutter, and sometimes words take longer. Please allow me to finish my answer.” Keep it short if that is all you want to share.

sections.heading: Bring the conversation back to your contribution
sections.body:
If interrupted, you can say, “There is one more part of that example I would like to explain.” If you need clarification, ask for it. A pause does not mean that you lack the answer.

After the interview, review whether you explained your strongest examples and understood the role. Write any follow-up questions. You can value your preparation even when the interview felt uncomfortable; one conversation does not define your abilities or your future options.

title: Talking about your stutter on your own terms
excerpt: Choose whether, when, and how much to share with classmates, colleagues, or friends.

sections.heading: Start with your purpose
sections.body:
Disclosure can be a practical request, a personal conversation, or something you decide not to do. You might want a tutor to allow more time, a friend to stop finishing sentences, or a group to understand a pause. Pick the purpose before deciding how much detail to give.

You can tell one person privately rather than announce it to a room. You can also change your mind later. Being open is not a test of courage, and privacy does not mean you are ashamed.

sections.heading: Try language you would actually use
sections.body:
• Short: “I stutter. Please give me time to finish.”
  • Practical: “Sometimes I pause on words. It helps if you do not fill them in.”
  • Personal: “I want to talk about how speaking has felt for me.”

Adapt these examples into Bangla, English, or the language that feels natural. You do not need clinical terminology or a polished explanation. You can write a message first if speaking about it feels difficult.

sections.heading: Decide what happens next
sections.body:
You can welcome questions or set a boundary: “I do not want advice right now; I just wanted you to know.” If someone offers a cure or a personal story, you can thank them without agreeing to try it.

Think about where you want this information shared. Ask a teacher or friend to check with you before telling others. Afterward, notice whether the conversation made the next interaction easier or revealed a support need. That is more useful than judging whether you disclosed perfectly.

title: Meeting new people without hiding your ideas
excerpt: Small, flexible ways to join conversations at university, clubs, and social events.

sections.heading: Choose a setting you want to be in
sections.body:
Shared activities give a conversation somewhere to begin. A programming club, study group, or volunteering session lets you ask about the task in front of you. Choose an activity you care about, rather than attending only to test your speech.

Set a small participation goal: introduce yourself to one person, ask about a project, or share a useful link. The goal can change once you arrive. You are allowed to listen, leave early, or try another event.

sections.heading: Give yourself several ways into the group
sections.body:
You can ask a friend to introduce you, join a smaller conversation, or message the organiser beforehand. If names feel pressured, use a name badge or write your name while still choosing to speak if you wish.

Simple openings include “How did you get involved?” and “What are you working on?” Use questions you are actually interested in. You do not have to keep every conversation going or entertain everyone you meet.

sections.heading: Measure connection, not performance
sections.body:
Afterward, ask whether you learned something about someone or shared something that mattered to you. A conversation with stuttering can still be warm, funny, and interesting. You can send a follow-up message about the shared activity.

If a group repeatedly rushes or mocks you, the problem deserves attention. Speak with the organiser or choose a more welcoming space. You do not need to earn basic respect by speaking differently. Consider peer support if you would like to meet others who understand the experience of stuttering.

title: Speaking in Bangla and English: a planning guide
excerpt: Bring both languages into support conversations and keep language choice personal.

sections.heading: Describe your real speaking day
sections.body:
A Bangladeshi student might discuss family matters in Bangla, present in English, and switch languages with friends. Write down where you use each language and which situations you want support with. This gives a therapist a more useful picture than one short conversation in a clinic.

You can note examples of difficult situations without recording yourself. If you do record a conversation, obtain permission from anyone included and keep the file private.

sections.heading: Ask how both languages will be considered
sections.body:
ASHA’s clinical guidance notes that exposure to another language does not increase the likelihood of developing stuttering. Assessment should consider multilingual experience rather than treating every hesitation in a less familiar language as stuttering.

Ask a provider whether they can work in Bangla and English, use an interpreter when needed, and distinguish language-learning demands from stuttering. Share your preferred terms and the language in which you want to discuss personal concerns.

sections.heading: Choose participation goals across your contexts
sections.body:
You might choose to ask a question in an English-medium class and explain an idea in Bangla to a relative. These are different communication tasks, so each can have its own preparation and support.

  • Keep technical vocabulary nearby when it helps.
  • Ask for clarification rather than guessing a word.
  • Use the language or mixture that fits the conversation.

You do not need to abandon a language because a particular day felt difficult. Discuss persistent concerns with a qualified speech-language professional who understands your language background.

title: Your first speech therapy appointment
excerpt: Prepare your questions, describe your priorities, and leave with a clear next step.

sections.heading: Bring the situations that matter
sections.body:
Write a short account of when you first noticed stuttering, any previous support, and what you want to do more comfortably. Include meaningful situations such as saying your name, answering a class question, or speaking with family. You do not need to demonstrate your most difficult speech to deserve support.

Bring relevant reports if you have them. Tell the therapist which languages you use and whether you prefer to attend alone or with a supporter.

sections.heading: Make room for your questions
sections.body:
• What experience do you have with people who stutter in my age group?
  • How will you learn about the impact on my life?
  • How will we choose goals together?
  • What will appointments and any home activities involve?
  • What are the fees, cancellation rules, and likely review points?

Ask for an explanation in everyday language when you need one. You can take notes or request a written outline so you do not have to remember everything during the appointment.

sections.heading: Leave knowing the next decision
sections.body:
Before leaving, check what the therapist recommends, why, and what alternatives are available. Ask when you will review whether the plan fits your goals. You can seek another opinion if you do not feel heard.

Our Bangladesh directory links to official provider pages and contact routes. It does not book an appointment or guarantee a particular therapist’s availability. Confirm age suitability, stuttering experience, costs, and appointment details directly before travelling.

title: Choosing therapy goals beyond fluency
excerpt: Turn everyday priorities into goals you can discuss and review with your therapist.

sections.heading: Name what you want your week to include
sections.body:
Instead of starting with “I must never stutter,” write an activity you want to take part in: explain a project, order your own meal, or speak during a meeting. Add what currently makes the activity difficult and what support you would find useful.

These notes can help you and a therapist discuss priorities. You may want to work on speech, physical effort, reactions, participation, or a combination. Your goals do not have to match someone else’s.

sections.heading: Make the goal observable and flexible
sections.body:
An example is: “At our next group meeting, I want to explain one design decision, with notes available and time to finish.” You can later ask whether you shared the idea, whether the support helped, and whether the task still matters to you.

Choose a review date together. A goal is a working agreement, so it can change if it feels exhausting, becomes irrelevant, or reveals a different need. You do not have to complete a rigid ladder to deserve progress.

sections.heading: Keep a brief record
sections.body:
• What did I want to communicate?
  • What did I try?
  • What felt comfortable or effortful?
  • What would I like to change with my therapist?

Use the editable tracker in Resources if it helps. Leave out private details you would not want stored on a shared device. A few useful observations are enough; tracking should not turn every conversation into an assessment.

title: Questions to ask about online speech therapy
excerpt: Check suitability, privacy, costs, and the practical setup before booking remotely.

sections.heading: Confirm the service before paying
sections.body:
Ask whether the provider offers remote appointments for someone of your age, location, and language background. A website mentioning online services does not necessarily mean that every clinician or programme is available to you.

Explain that you are seeking support for stuttering. Ask about the clinician’s qualifications and experience, the assessment process, fees, payment route, cancellation policy, and what happens if the connection fails.

sections.heading: Make privacy part of the conversation
sections.body:
Ask which platform will be used, whether sessions are recorded, where records are kept, and how you will receive documents. If you share a home, discuss a realistic way to get privacy. Headphones may help with listening, but they do not stop someone nearby from hearing your voice.

Agree on how a parent or supporter may join when appropriate. You should know who is present at both ends of the appointment.

sections.heading: Test the basics and keep a backup
sections.body:
• Check the microphone, speaker, and connection.
  • Keep a charger and a way to contact reception nearby.
  • Put your questions where you can see them.
  • Agree whether a dropped call will be resumed or rescheduled.

After the first appointment, consider whether you could explain your concerns and understood the plan. Discuss any audio delays or accessibility needs with the therapist. This checklist helps you ask informed questions; it does not establish that remote care is suitable for every person or every clinical need.

title: A calmer listening space for your child
excerpt: Practical conversation habits for parents and carers, without pressure to speak a certain way.

sections.heading: Make room for the message
sections.body:
Choose a short time when you can give your child your attention without competing tasks. Let the conversation follow something they enjoy. You do not need a special exercise or a lesson about speech; you can talk about a picture, a game, or the day.

Wait for their turn to end before responding. If you miss a detail, ask about the meaning. Try to keep your reaction warm and ordinary rather than visibly celebrating only moments of fluent speech.

sections.heading: Invite feelings without demanding a conversation
sections.body:
If your child mentions difficulty speaking, acknowledge it in simple language. You might ask, “Would you like me to listen, or is there something you want help with?” Follow their lead and avoid questioning them repeatedly about how much they stuttered at school.

Explain your listening preferences to relatives so the child does not have to manage everyone’s advice. Ask siblings to take turns and allow everyone time to finish.

sections.heading: Seek advice when you are concerned
sections.body:
Write down your questions for a qualified speech-language professional. Ask how they assess children and involve families. Share what your child enjoys and what seems difficult, as well as any school concerns.

You do not have to decide on your own whether an assessment is needed. Contact a qualified provider for advice when concerned rather than relying on a promise that a particular exercise will fix speech. Our Bangladesh directory marks child-focused services so you can start by asking the right department.

title: A classroom checklist for teachers
excerpt: Agree on participation, turn-taking, and assessment with the student who stutters.

sections.heading: Ask privately instead of guessing
sections.body:
Invite the student to explain what helps them participate. You might ask about answering the register, reading aloud, group work, and presentations. Do not assume that a quiet student wants to avoid every speaking task or that a confident student needs no support.

Agree on how you will revisit the plan. A student may prefer one arrangement in a small seminar and another in a large lecture. Check before discussing their stutter with classmates.

sections.heading: Make discussion easier to enter
sections.body:
• Use clear turn-taking and discourage interruptions.
  • Allow thinking and speaking time.
  • Offer ways to contribute through speech, writing, or a diagram when the learning objective allows.
  • Discuss reading order and presentation format beforehand.

When marking an answer, separate subject understanding from assumptions about fluency. Ask your institution how to document and approve any formal assessment arrangement. The examples here are teaching suggestions, not a description of Bangladeshi legal requirements.

sections.heading: Respond to reactions in the room
sections.body:
Address mocking or imitation promptly through the school’s procedures. Check privately with the student about what they need, rather than asking them to teach the whole class in the moment.

Review what is working after a real lesson. “Did you have enough time to explain your answer?” is more useful than “Was your speech good today?” Collaboration with the student, family where appropriate, and their clinician can help keep support practical and consistent.

title: Responding to teasing and speech-based bullying
excerpt: Plan support, preserve useful details, and choose a response that feels safe.

sections.heading: You do not have to manage it alone
sections.body:
Mocking someone’s speech is a problem to address, even when the person calls it a joke. Decide who can help: a trusted teacher, parent, club organiser, supervisor, or student welfare contact. Tell them what happened and what you need next.

You can leave an interaction or ask a friend to stay with you. You do not have to confront someone, explain stuttering publicly, or deliver a clever reply to make your concern valid.

sections.heading: Keep a factual record if useful
sections.body:
Write the date, place, what was said or done, and any witnesses. For online harassment, save relevant screenshots if doing so is safe, then use the platform’s reporting and blocking controls. Avoid repeatedly rereading hurtful messages.

Share the record with the person handling your report. Ask who will see it, what the next step is, and when you can expect an update. Follow your school or organisation’s reporting route and ask for help if you cannot find it.

sections.heading: Choose your own words and boundaries
sections.body:
If you want a short response, try, “Please do not imitate my speech,” or “I want to finish what I was saying.” You may also say nothing and move toward support. Different situations call for different choices.

Afterward, spend time with someone who treats you with respect. If the experience keeps affecting your sleep, studies, or willingness to participate, consider talking with a qualified mental health professional. You deserve support with the impact as well as a response to the behaviour.

title: When speaking worries take over your preparation
excerpt: Separate the task from the worry and choose one manageable next step.

sections.heading: Write the concern as a sentence
sections.body:
Before a conversation, it can help to name what you are worried about: “They might interrupt,” “I might forget my example,” or “I do not know how long I will have.” Each concern points to a different practical question.

Separate what you can arrange from what you cannot predict. You can bring notes, ask about timing, or contact a supportive person. You cannot guarantee every listener’s reaction or require your speech to follow a script.

sections.heading: Pick one useful action
sections.body:
Choose a small action connected to your purpose. That might be sending a tutor a request, rehearsing the order of a presentation, or asking a friend to listen. Set a stopping point for preparation so you still have time for meals, rest, and other work.

You are allowed to change the plan or take a break. If an activity feels overwhelming, do not force yourself through it to prove something. Discuss a manageable approach with a professional if you need support.

sections.heading: Ask for support with the worry itself
sections.body:
Speech therapy and mental health support can address different needs. If worry is repeatedly restricting your daily life, describe that impact to a qualified professional and ask what support is appropriate. You do not need to wait until you can explain it perfectly.

This is an everyday planning guide, not a treatment for anxiety. You can use the journal in Resources to capture a few observations for a support conversation, without monitoring every feeling or judging yourself for having one.

title: After a difficult conversation: a kinder review
excerpt: Reflect on what happened without turning one interaction into a judgment about yourself.

sections.heading: Separate the event from the verdict
sections.body:
A difficult interaction can leave you replaying a few seconds and overlooking everything else. Try writing only what happened: “I gave my name, paused, and the receptionist asked me to repeat it.” Then notice any wider conclusion you added, such as “I should never make calls.”

You do not have to argue yourself into feeling positive. The aim is a more complete account, including the task you completed, the listener’s behaviour, and what you needed.

sections.heading: Choose a useful response now
sections.body:
Ask what would help in the next hour. You might want a break, a message to a friend, something to eat, or a different activity. You can decide later whether the conversation needs a practical follow-up.

  • What did I manage to communicate?
  • What was difficult or outside my control?
  • What would I say to a friend in the same situation?
  • Is there one support request I want to make?

sections.heading: Keep the next step small
sections.body:
You can return to the activity with different support, choose another route, or discuss it with a therapist. None of those choices requires pretending the experience was easy.

If replaying conversations is repeatedly taking over your day, bring that pattern to a qualified mental health professional. A journal is an optional reflection tool, not a replacement for care. You are allowed to put the notebook away when writing stops being useful and starts feeling like another test.

title: Finding a peer group that fits you
excerpt: Questions to ask about age, privacy, accessibility, and participation before joining.

sections.heading: Decide what you hope to find
sections.body:
You may want to hear other experiences, meet people your age, discuss school, or simply spend time somewhere stuttering is understood. A peer group can offer connection without being a clinical service. You do not need to arrive with a story ready to tell.

Read the organiser’s description and ask how a first meeting works. Some groups permit listening without speaking; others have a structured activity. Check rather than assuming every group follows the same format.

sections.heading: Check the details that affect you
sections.body:
• Is it for children, teens, adults, or families?
  • Who facilitates and how are disagreements handled?
  • Are meetings recorded, and who can attend?
  • What language is used?
  • Are there fees or registration requirements?
  • What time is the meeting in Bangladesh?

International websites may offer virtual programmes, but location eligibility and schedules can change. For children and teenagers, a parent or carer should review the group’s safeguarding and participation arrangements.

sections.heading: Let the first visit be information
sections.body:
After a meeting, consider whether you felt respected, had choices about participation, and understood the privacy expectations. You can try another group or decide group support is not what you want right now.

Resources links to Friends and the National Stuttering Association, both US-based organisations, as starting points for exploring their current programmes. A listing is not a guarantee that a particular meeting accepts participants from Bangladesh. Ask the organiser before sharing personal details or booking anything.

title: Stuttering myths: questions worth asking
excerpt: A short, sourced guide to causes, variability, and claims about a cure.

sections.heading: Is stuttering just nervousness?
sections.body:
No. NIDCD describes developmental stuttering as involving multiple interacting factors, with genetic contributions and differences observed in brain research. Feeling nervous is not an adequate explanation for why someone stutters.

Speech can vary by situation. That variability does not mean a person is choosing to stutter or trying less hard.

sections.heading: Does more effort guarantee fluent speech?
sections.body:
Someone can know exactly what they want to say and still experience repetitions, stretched sounds, or blocks. Listeners should allow time and attend to the message rather than interpreting a pause as lack of knowledge.

A useful question is, “What would help this person participate?” Avoid making fluent speech a condition for respect.

sections.heading: Is there one guaranteed cure?
sections.body:
NIDCD states that there is no current cure, while treatment options can help people manage stuttering. Be cautious about promises of certainty or a fixed recovery deadline.

Before paying for a programme, ask who provides it, what evidence supports its claims, what outcomes it measures, and how limitations and costs are explained.

title: How to read a stuttering treatment claim
excerpt: A practical checklist for separating an interesting finding from a promise that applies to everyone.

sections.heading: Find the exact claim
sections.body:
Copy the headline into your notes, then look for the original study or clinical guidance it cites. “Participants improved on a measure” is a different claim from “this cures everyone.” Check whether the page is describing a study, selling a service, or sharing one person’s experience.

A testimonial can tell you what someone valued. It cannot, by itself, establish what will happen for another person. Look for a clear distinction between the two.

sections.heading: Ask how the result was obtained
sections.body:
• Who took part, and how many people were included?
  • Were their ages and circumstances similar to yours?
  • Was there a comparison group?
  • What changed: speech frequency, effort, participation, or wellbeing?
  • Were outcomes checked after the programme ended?
  • Were limitations and possible conflicts of interest disclosed?

You do not need advanced statistics to ask these questions. If an article omits the details, follow its references or ask the provider to explain.

sections.heading: Use evidence in a personal discussion
sections.body:
Write down the outcome you care about and bring the claim to a qualified clinician. Ask what is known, what is uncertain, and how they would assess whether an approach is useful for you.

ASHA’s clinical practice portal is a professional starting point with references, not a personalised prescription. A responsible support conversation should leave room for your preferences and for uncertainty. You can take time to decide before committing money or agreeing to a programme.

title: Using recordings, apps, and digital tools thoughtfully
excerpt: Keep tools optional, protect recordings, and ask what a product actually measures.

sections.heading: Choose a job for the tool
sections.body:
A voice memo might help you remember a presentation idea. A calendar can remind you of an appointment. A notes app can hold questions for a therapist. Start with a practical purpose instead of assuming that more speech data always means better support.

You can prepare and reflect without recording yourself at all. If listening back makes you repeatedly judge your speech, discuss another approach with your therapist or set the recording aside.

sections.heading: Check where your information goes
sections.body:
Before using an app, read what it collects, whether audio leaves your device, how recordings can be deleted, and whether paid features renew automatically. Do not upload another person’s voice without their permission.

Use a private device where possible. Avoid keeping sensitive recordings in a shared folder. Give a file an ordinary name that does not reveal someone else’s personal information.

sections.heading: Treat scores as product outputs
sections.body:
If an app labels speech as good, bad, fluent, or successful, ask what it measures and whether that measure matches your own goal. An automated score is not a complete account of your communication or a clinical assessment.

  • Check the cancellation and refund rules before paying.
  • Ask a qualified professional about treatment claims.
  • Keep an alternative if a tool is unavailable.

The downloads on Fluent Minds work without an account. The personal speaking plan is generated in your browser; you decide where to save or share it.

title: Build a personal communication support plan
excerpt: Put your preferences, useful scripts, and next steps on one page you control.

sections.heading: Pick three real situations
sections.body:
Choose situations from your week, such as a class, a family conversation, and an appointment. For each, write what you want to communicate and what would make the exchange more accessible. Keep the plan short enough to use.

You might want time to finish, written appointment details, a quieter space, or a chance to prepare a question. Preferences can differ across settings, so avoid turning one useful choice into a rule for every conversation.

sections.heading: Choose what to share and with whom
sections.body:
A private plan can hold detailed reflections. A version for a teacher or colleague can contain only the request they need to know. You do not have to include your medical history.

For example: “Please let me complete my answer before the next question. If time runs short, tell me so we can agree on a way to finish.” Ask the listener whether they understand the request and what is possible in that setting.

sections.heading: Make it a living document
sections.body:
• One thing I want to participate in this week.
  • One support request I can make.
  • One person I can contact if I need help.
  • A date to review what worked.

Use the speaking-plan download in Practice or the support-plan worksheet in Resources. Store it somewhere you control, especially on a shared computer. Update it when your priorities change. The plan can support a discussion with a qualified therapist, but it does not need to look like a clinical form to be useful.

title: Breathing for comfort: options and limits
excerpt: Optional comfort ideas and questions for your therapist, without promises about fluency.

sections.heading: Begin with ordinary breathing
sections.body: If you want a moment to settle, sit comfortably and notice a few ordinary breaths. You do not need to take a very deep breath or change your speech. Stop an exercise if you feel uncomfortable or lightheaded.

sections.heading: Separate comfort from speech treatment
sections.body: Breathing exercises are not a cure for stuttering. A speech-language professional can discuss whether any breathing or speech strategies fit your needs. You do not need to control every breath before you are allowed to speak.

sections.heading: Skip rigid breath holding
sections.body: You can choose an ordinary pause instead of following a timed breathing pattern. If you have a health condition or symptoms related to breathing, ask your healthcare professional what is appropriate.

sections.heading: Prepare the situation too
sections.body: Keep water and notes available for a presentation, check the microphone, and ask for time to finish your point. Practical changes to the setting can be part of your plan.

sections.heading: Listeners can offer time
sections.body: If you are supporting someone else, avoid instructing them to breathe or relax while they speak. Wait for their message and ask privately what kind of support they prefer.

sections.heading: Choose a useful next step
sections.body: Write one question for a therapist or one support request for an upcoming conversation. The daily practice page helps you create a participation goal that does not depend on fluent speech.

title: Easy onsets: a strategy to discuss with a therapist
excerpt: Understand the idea of a gentle voice start and why individual guidance matters.

sections.heading: What the term describes
sections.body: Easy onset refers to a gradual start of voicing and is one of several speech modification strategies discussed in clinical fluency guidance. It is not a complete explanation of stuttering or a guarantee against blocks.

sections.heading: Ask for individual demonstration
sections.body: If a therapist recommends the strategy, ask them to demonstrate it, explain its purpose, and help you try it comfortably in the languages you use. Avoid adding force or pressing on your throat. You can stop and ask questions.

sections.heading: Discuss effort and usefulness
sections.body: Tell your therapist if using a strategy feels tiring, unnatural, or distracting. Agree on when you want to use it and how you will review whether it helps with your own communication goals.

sections.heading: Keep other goals in view
sections.body: Your plan can include listener support, participation, and reactions to stuttering as well as speech strategies. You should not have to use a technique to earn time to finish a sentence.

sections.heading: Prepare for a support conversation
sections.body: Bring one situation you want help with to an appointment. Ask what alternatives exist and how the therapist will adapt their approach if a technique does not suit you. No fixed improvement deadline applies to everyone.

title: Voluntary stuttering: choice, context, and support
excerpt: An introduction to an optional therapy activity, with attention to consent and comfort.

sections.heading: Different people want different support
sections.body: Some people want help with their reactions to stuttering or with situations they avoid. Others have different priorities. Your preferences should guide the discussion rather than a requirement to complete a particular activity.

sections.heading: What voluntary stuttering means
sections.body: The term describes deliberately producing a stuttering-like moment. It may be discussed within individualised therapy, but it is optional and is not a cure or a test of confidence.

sections.heading: Discuss the activity before trying it
sections.body: Ask a qualified speech-language professional why they suggest it, what alternatives exist, and how you can stop or change the task. You do not need to practise with strangers or in a situation that feels unsafe.

sections.heading: Review your own response
sections.body: If you choose an activity with a therapist, discuss how it felt and whether it served your goal. Do not assume that another person’s positive experience predicts your own. An uncomfortable task can be adapted or declined.

sections.heading: For friends and teachers
sections.body: Do not ask someone to demonstrate a stutter for entertainment, surprise them with a speaking challenge, or assign this activity yourself. Ask how they prefer to be supported and respect the answer.
